/TUESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
Issued at 400 PM CDT Mon Aug 17 2026

Heat:

A plume of southwesterly winds push back across the Central 
Plains towards our area ahead of lee cyclogenesis in western 
Kansas on Tuesday, bringing back warm air to the region. A warm
front should start pushing into our area from the southwest by 
Tuesday afternoon, increasing our temperatures back into the 90s
areawide. Far western and southern portions of our area will 
likely breach 100 degrees, bringing heat indices back into the 
105-110 degree range for Tuesday. For that reason, our Kansas 
counties and the far western tier of our Missouri counties as 
well as some of our Missouri counties along the Arkansas border 
have been added to a new Heat Advisory from 1 PM to 8 PM on 
Tuesday. Depending on the speed and timing of the warm front, it
is possible an eastward expansion of the Advisory may be needed
in subsequent forecast packages. 

The presence of convection during the day on Wednesday will have
implications on temperatures (and thus heat indices) and whether
or not areas reach Heat Advisory criteria again on Wednesday. It
is likely to be a similar area to Tuesday where heat indices 
may meet or exceed 105 degrees on Wednesday, especially if
convection remains confined to areas east of Interstate 49 as is
currently expected. This uncertainty prevented Heat Advisory
issuance for Wednesday at this point, though it may or may not
need to be added in coming days. Additional heat concerns
continue through the week, with the four days of 100+ heat
indices criteria potentially being met in the western and
southern portions of our area, leading to the potential for
additional Heat Advisory issuance through at least Friday.
However, Tuesday and Wednesday's convection will have
implications on the pattern for the rest of the week, so that
will be something to watch closely if in heat-sensitive
industries or outdoors this week.


Severe Weather Risk Tuesday Night/Wednesday Morning:

Very late Tuesday night into early Wednesday morning, an MCS is
progged to develop along the nose of the nocturnal LLJ as a
shortwave moves across northern Missouri. The lee cyclogenesis
in Kansas will also help to sustain isentropic ascent during 
the overnight hours, though the primary question regarding this
overnight MCS remains what the forcing mechanism will be that
initiates the complex that moves into our area. Another storm 
complex further north into Nebraska may influence how conditions
evolve throughout the day, though it does appear likely that 
this northern MCS will send an outflow boundary surging south 
into central Missouri that will be the likely initiation 
mechanism for storms in our area. Storms appear to initiate 
north and west of our area in Kansas before moving into western 
Missouri, with most CAMs that initiate this activity indicating 
that storms organize into clusters by the time they reach our 
area. 

With the boost in the LLJ to 30-40 kts overnight, 0-3km bulk
shear values increase to 50-60kts by 12Z Wednesday, which would
support strong cold pool development and damaging wind gusts
with this cluster of storms. Hodographs are sufficiently curved
that there may be a conditional threat for QLCS tornado
development as well, especially as storms progress south and
east and approach the warm front spread across the area. Best 
severe chances remain along and northwest of the greater Lake of
the Ozarks/Truman Lake corridor, which is within the Slight 
Risk (Level 2 of 5) area from SPC.


Severe Weather Risk Wednesday:

Scattered showers and storms may continue on and off during the
day on Wednesday after the progression of the late Tuesday night
system, but the 12Z model suite is increasingly pointing 
towards another area of severe weather potential on Wednesday 
evening/night across portions of southern Missouri into 
northern Arkansas as the shortwave aloft progresses from Kansas
into Missouri. Southern portions of the state have the best 
instability available (1000-2000 J/kg MUCAPE) as the nocturnal 
LLJ ramps back up. An MCS appears to be the most likely cause of
severe weather, with the primary threat being damaging winds 
during the evening/overnight hours as storms become more 
organized. However, storms may initially form as supercells or 
supercell-like clusters in southwest Missouri, with straight 
hodographs during the afternoon to early evening hours 
suggesting initial storms may be prone to splitting. As such, 
cannot fully rule out hail with strongest afternoon storms. 
30-40kts of 0-3km shear could again support mesovortices 
embedded within the larger storm clusters, especially once the 
LLJ begins increasing low-level hodograph curvature. As the 
nocturnal LLJ ramps up, storms should become more organized into
a bowing segment(s) as cold pools organize along the LLJ and 
shear strengthens, where the damaging wind threat is most likely
to materialize.
